lesson.menu_desc: The words of a deal -- acquire, merge, target, due diligence, valuation, stake, bid, synergy, divest, letter of intent -- and the future forms that carry a deal timeline: will, be going to and the present continuous -- 27 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 -- M&A Vocabulary -- The Words of a Deal
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Simone Quiles de Santana Marques | Lesson 21 -- M&A Vocabulary
lesson.grammar_point: future forms for a deal timeline (will / be going to / present continuous)

listenings.text: Simone, this is Michael Reed from the buyer side, with a quick note before our call on Monday. Here is where we are. Our client is going to acquire a logistics company in Campinas, and your team will run the Brazilian side of the transaction. The target is smaller than us, so this is an acquisition, not a merger of equals. A few dates for your diary. We are signing the letter of intent next Friday, and due diligence starts the Monday after that. The financial valuation is already with the bank, so what we need from you is the legal review. I should warn you about one thing. The seller is going to keep a minority stake of fifteen percent for two years, and they are not going to divest it early, whatever they say in the room. Finally, the board will want a note on synergy before they approve the price, so please keep your comments on the contract separate from the commercial argument. Talk on Monday.

It is Sunday evening and I am planning my week around this transaction. Tomorrow I am meeting the finance team at nine to understand the valuation, because I cannot review a price I do not understand. On Tuesday I am reading the letter of intent line by line, and I already know what I am looking for: the exclusivity period, the confidentiality clause, and whether the document says it is not binding. Due diligence will take six weeks, and honestly it is going to be longer, because the target has three companies inside it and nobody has looked at the property files since two thousand and nineteen. My plan for the language is simple. When the date is fixed and in the diary, I will use the present continuous: we are signing on Friday. When it is a plan or an intention, I will use going to: they are going to keep a minority stake. And when it is a prediction or a promise I make in the room, I will use will: due diligence will take six weeks, and I will send you the report on the tenth.

extra_audio.text: First, the buyer identifies a target and asks the bank for a valuation of the business. Then, the two sides sign a letter of intent that sets out the price and the timetable, but is not yet binding. After that, the legal team runs due diligence and reads every contract and every property file inside the target. Next, the buyer makes a formal bid, and the parties argue about the price, about the stake the seller keeps, and about the synergy the deal is supposed to create. Finally, the buyer signs the contract and acquires the company, and the seller divests the part of the business it no longer wants.
